A2.3 Data Transmission

Topic A2: Networks | Packets, Protocols & Paths

Retrieval Practice

Recall A2.2 (Network Architecture) before we dive into protocols.

  1. What’s the key difference between a switch and a router?
  2. What is the purpose of a gateway?
  3. Give one drawback of client–server architecture.

Press Down for answers

Answer 1

What’s the key difference between a switch and a router?

Switches forward within a LAN using MAC addresses; routers forward between networks using IP addresses.

Answer 2

What is the purpose of a gateway?

To translate between different protocols/systems so disparate networks can communicate.

Answer 3

Give one drawback of client–server architecture.

The server can become a single point of failure (and a performance bottleneck).

The Big Question

🤔 You click a link and a web page loads.

But the internet is messy: delays, failures, rerouting…

So why does it usually work?

❌ Misconception: “Data travels as one continuous stream on a fixed path.”

That would be fragile: one failure would break the entire transmission.

✅ Reality: data is split into packets and routed independently.

Protocols add structure (encapsulation) and reliability (checksums, sequencing, retransmission).

HL The TCP/IP Model

How can billions of devices communicate if everyone follows a layered set of rules?

The TCP/IP model organises networking into layers.

Each layer adds information (headers) to support delivery and interpretation.

Press Down for the layers

Application Layer

Purpose: formats data for user applications.

Examples: HTTP/HTTPS (web), SMTP (email), FTP (file transfer).

Transport Layer

Purpose: end-to-end communication between applications.

Protocols: TCP or UDP.

Data unit: segment.

Internet Layer

Purpose: routing between networks.

Protocol: IP (Internet Protocol).

Data unit: packet.

Network Interface Layer

Purpose: local delivery over a physical link (Ethernet/Wi‑Fi).

Uses: MAC addressing and physical transmission.

Data unit: frame.

HL Encapsulation

How does data “gain” the information needed to travel across networks?

Encapsulation wraps data with headers at each layer.

Data becomes: segments → packets → frames.

Headers include

Addresses, ports, sequencing, checksums, protocol IDs…

Decapsulation

At the receiver, headers are removed layer-by-layer to recover the original data.

🧠 Quick Check

At which layer does data become a “packet”?

Internet layer — IP adds its header to create a packet.

HL TCP vs UDP

When do we prefer reliability — and when do we prefer speed?
AspectTCPUDP
ConnectionConnection-orientedConnectionless
DeliveryReliable, orderedBest-effort, may reorder/lose
OverheadHigherLower
Typical useWeb pages, file transferLive streaming, gaming, DNS

🧠 Quick Check

Which protocol is usually better for downloading a file correctly?

TCP — reliability and correct ordering matter more than minimal overhead.

Packet Switching

Why do packets sometimes arrive out of order — and why is that okay?

Packet switching splits data into packets that may take different routes.

MTU is a typical upper limit (often ~1500 bytes on Ethernet).

A header contains routing and reassembly metadata.

Key fields

Sequence numbers (reassembly)

Checksums (error detection)

🧠 Quick Check

Do packets always arrive in the order they were sent?

No. Packets can take different routes; sequencing enables correct reassembly.

HL TCP 3‑Way Handshake

How does TCP establish a reliable connection before data transfer?

1) SYN — client requests a connection.

2) SYN‑ACK — server acknowledges and synchronises.

3) ACK — client acknowledges; connection established.

HL Subnetting & CIDR Logic

How do we determine which part of an IP identifies the network?

A subnet mask marks network bits vs host bits.

Network address = IP AND subnet mask.

Example (conceptual): 192.168.1.130 with mask 255.255.255.0 → network 192.168.1.0

HL NAT (Network Address Translation)

How can many devices share one public IPv4 address?

NAT maps many private IPs to one public IP.

Why: conserves IPv4 addresses and hides internal addressing.

Private vs Public

Private IP: used inside a LAN (e.g., 192.168.x.x)

Public IP: globally routable address on the internet

Misconception Check

A. Encapsulation means encrypting data as it moves through layers.

B. Packet switching guarantees packets arrive in order.

C. TCP provides reliable ordered delivery (at the cost of overhead).

D. NAT can allow many private devices to share one public IP.

Press Down for answers

Answers

A: False. Encapsulation adds headers; encryption is a separate security mechanism.

B: False. Packets can take different routes and arrive out of order.

C: True. TCP adds sequencing, acknowledgements, and retransmission.

D: True. NAT maps private addresses to a public one.

Key Takeaways

  • HL TCP/IP layers structure communication and support encapsulation/decapsulation.
  • Transport choices matter: TCP (reliable) vs UDP (low overhead).
  • Packet switching uses headers, sequencing, and checksums to survive network unpredictability.
  • HL Subnetting and NAT explain how addressing works at scale.
